intro: Looking for a corporation tax accountant near you usually means your company has a return to prepare or a tax position you want handled properly by someone you can actually reach. You may be a director filing for the first time, or you may simply want someone local to talk through profits, reliefs and deadlines. iComply introduces you to a suitable UK accountant who quotes you directly, with the price on application.
need_heading: What people searching for a corporation tax accountant near me usually need
need_lead: Most people behind this search want a local accountant who understands company tax and can take the return off their hands.
needs: You have set up a limited company and need to understand when corporation tax is due and what has to be filed.
Your year end has passed and the company tax return still needs preparing, so you want an accountant to calculate taxable profits and submit it.
You are unsure whether your company qualifies for reliefs such as capital allowances or R&D and want that looked at before the return is filed.
You would rather deal with an accountant you can meet or speak to locally than post documents to a firm you have never met.
Your profits sit in the range where marginal relief may apply and you want the calculation done correctly.
context_heading: Understanding who you are dealing with
context: In the UK the word accountant on its own is not a protected title, so anyone can call themselves one. Titles such as Chartered Accountant, Chartered Certified Accountant and Chartered Management Accountant are protected, and members are bound by their body's ethics, training and complaints rules.

Every practice offering accountancy services must also be supervised for anti-money-laundering purposes, either by a professional body or by HMRC. It is reasonable to ask which body supervises a firm, whether they hold professional indemnity insurance and how complaints are handled. iComply is not regulated and does not give tax advice itself; it introduces you to an accountant who does.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Say that you are looking for a corporation tax accountant near you and give the town or area you want them to be based in.
Describe your company, including what it does and whether it has traded for a full year or is newly formed.
Give your company's year end date and say whether the return has been filed before or is still outstanding.
Mention whether you already keep records and accounts, or whether you need those prepared as part of the work.
Explain whether you think any reliefs such as capital allowances or R&D might apply to your company.
Say how you would prefer to work with the accountant, such as meeting in person locally or dealing with things remotely.
questions: Which professional body supervises your practice for anti-money-laundering purposes?
Do you hold professional indemnity insurance, and how are complaints handled?
What do you need from me to calculate my company's taxable profits and prepare the company tax return?
Will you check whether my company is eligible for R&D relief or capital allowances?
How will you work out whether marginal relief applies to my profits?
What is your quote for preparing and filing the corporation tax return, and what does it include?

faqs.q: When is corporation tax usually due?
faqs.a: Corporation tax is usually due nine months and one day after your company's year end. The return itself has its own filing deadline, so it is worth confirming both dates with your accountant early.

faqs.q: Should I ask about R&D relief?
faqs.a: Yes, it is worth asking whether your company's work could qualify for R&D relief, as it can affect the tax you pay. Your accountant can look at your activities and tell you whether a claim is possible.

Marginal relief applies between certain profit thresholds, so the rate of corporation tax rises gradually rather than jumping straight to the higher rate. Your accountant can work out whether it affects your company.

faqs.q: How do I check an accountant is properly supervised?
faqs.a: Ask which professional body or HMRC supervises the practice for anti-money-laundering purposes, and whether they hold professional indemnity insurance. You can also check whether any protected titles they use, such as Chartered Accountant, are held with the relevant body.

extra_heading: What to expect at a first meeting about corporation tax
extra: When you first meet a corporation tax accountant near you, they will usually ask for your company's year end date, its accounts or records, and details of any income and expenses. This helps them calculate taxable profits and identify reliefs such as capital allowances or R&D that may apply. They may also check whether marginal relief affects your company, depending on its profits.

It is worth asking how they will keep you informed about deadlines, as corporation tax is usually due nine months and one day after your year end, and the return has its own filing date. A local accountant can explain these dates clearly and help you avoid penalties. You can also ask what records you need to keep and for how long.

Before the meeting, gather your company's registration details, recent bank statements, and any previous returns. This preparation helps the accountant give you a more accurate quote and a clearer picture of what needs doing. Remember that iComply introduces you to an accountant who quotes you directly; we do not provide tax advice ourselves.

extra_faqs.q: What should I bring to a first meeting with a corporation tax accountant?
extra_faqs.a: Bring your company's year end date, recent accounts or records of income and expenses, and any previous corporation tax returns. Also have your company registration details and bank statements to hand. This helps the accountant understand your position and quote accurately.

extra_faqs.q: How can I check an accountant is qualified to handle corporation tax?
extra_faqs.a: Ask which professional body supervises the practice for anti-money-laundering purposes and whether they hold professional indemnity insurance. You can also check if they use protected titles such as Chartered Accountant, Chartered Certified Accountant or Chartered Management Accountant, and verify membership with the relevant body.
